q: What is the difference between noble rot and grey rot?
opts: Noble rot affects only red grapes, grey rot only whites
Grey rot is a bacterium and noble rot is a fungus
Noble rot only develops in the cellar after fermentation
One fungus, benign in some conditions and spoiling in others
exp: Both are Botrytis cinerea. On healthy ripe white grapes with alternating damp and dry it concentrates sugar nobly; on damaged or wet fruit it simply spoils it.

q: Which condition is spread by sharpshooter insects and is a serious threat in parts of California?
exp: Pierce's disease is caused by the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa, carried by sharpshooters, and it blocks the vine's water-conducting tissue. There is no cure.

q: The traditional Bordeaux mixture used against mildew is based on which compound?
exp: Bordeaux mixture is copper sulphate with slaked lime. It is permitted in organic viticulture, though accumulating copper in soil is a live concern.

q: Hail is particularly feared because it
opts: can destroy fruit and damage wood in minutes
is easily prevented by netting at scale
exp: A hailstorm can strip a vineyard in a few minutes, and wounded wood invites disease into later seasons. Its local, unpredictable nature makes it hard to insure against.

q: In standard white winemaking, when does pressing usually occur?
exp: White grapes are normally pressed first and the juice fermented off its skins. Red wine ferments on skins to extract colour and tannin, then is pressed.

q: Cool fermentation temperatures are used for aromatic whites mainly to
exp: Cooler ferments keep volatile aromatic compounds from being driven off and favour fresh fruit character. They also run more slowly.

q: What is lees stirring, or batonnage?
opts: Filtering the wine through the spent skins
Racking the wine off its sediment repeatedly
Stirring the yeast sediment back into the wine
exp: Stirring the fine lees back into suspension builds texture and a savoury, bready character, and gives some protection against oxidation.

q: Malolactic conversion changes which acid into which?
exp: Bacteria convert sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering perceived acidity and often adding a creamy note. It is routine for reds and optional for whites.

q: Brief skin contact before pressing a white wine is used to
opts: strip every trace of colour out of the juice
extract aroma compounds from the skins
keep the juice from fermenting before it is pressed
raise the acidity of the juice before pressing
exp: A short maceration pulls aromatic compounds sitting in the skins into the juice. Pushed too far it also pulls tannin and coarseness.

q: A winemaker presses red grapes on arrival and ferments the juice with no skin contact. What is the most likely result?
opts: A wine that will not ferment
A wine unusually high in tannin
exp: Almost all grape pulp is pale, so colour comes from macerating juice with skins. Press red grapes straight away and the wine is barely coloured, which is how blanc de noirs is made.

q: What are punching down and pumping over used to manage?
opts: Sediment left in the finished bottle
The dosage added to sparkling wine
The temperature of the cellar during ageing
exp: Carbon dioxide pushes skins into a floating cap. Punching it down or pumping juice over it keeps skins wet and extraction going, and prevents the cap drying and spoiling.

q: Compared with white wine, red wine is generally fermented at
exp: Warmer ferments help extract colour and tannin from skins. Whites are kept cooler to protect aromatics, which is the opposite priority.

q: Whole uncrushed clusters are sealed under carbon dioxide, and fermentation begins inside the intact berries. Which technique is this?
exp: Whole clusters ferment intracellularly under carbon dioxide before being pressed. It gives bright colour, low tannin and the distinctive aromatics of Beaujolais.

opts: blending press wine back into free-run wine
bleeding off part of the juice early
adding water to the must to bring the alcohol down
fermenting the wine in sealed clay amphorae
exp: Running off part of the juice early raises the skin-to-juice ratio in what remains, concentrating the red. The drawn-off juice is commonly made into rose.

q: Extended maceration after fermentation has finished is used to
opts: settle the gross lees out before the wine is pressed
restart a fermentation that has stuck
drive off volatile acidity picked up in fermentation
exp: Leaving wine on skins after the sugar is gone continues to shape tannin, with harsher tannins tending to polymerise and settle out. It is a stylistic choice with real risk.

q: New oak barrels contribute which characteristics compared with older barrels?
opts: More overt oak flavour and tannin
exp: A new barrel gives vanilla, spice and toast plus some tannin. Barrels lose that influence with each use, and after a few fills act mainly as vessels.
